title: Pre-allocating Massive Fixed-Size Static Buffers to Avoid Allocator
damaged_code:
```rust
// Rust
static mut BUFFER: [u8; 10_000_000] = [0; 10_000_000]; // 10MB static array
```
pattern: Declaring huge fixed-size global arrays or arrays on the stack (`[T; N]`) to completely avoid heap allocator overhead.
why_bad: Huge static buffers bloat the executable's binary size and resident set size (RSS), causing cold-start delay due to virtual memory page faults when first accessed. If done on the stack, it easily triggers catastrophic stack overflows [111, 317].
detection: Static or thread-local byte arrays initialized with very large dimensions (e.g., > 1 MB) without dynamic heap backing.
counterexample: Embedded systems or microcontrollers with no operating system or heap allocator where absolute fixed-size memory maps are mandatory. `Contextual`.
fix:
```rust
let buffer = vec![0u8; 10_000_000]; // Dynamically allocated on heap
```
source: *Systems Performance*, Chapter 2 (p. 111); *A Philosophy of Software Design*, Chapter 20 (p. 317).
